source.title: Mamba as Decision Maker: Exploring Multi-scale Sequence Modeling in Offline Reinforcement Learning
source.authors: Jia-Hang Cao; Qiang Zhang; Ziqing Wang; Jing-Kai Sun; Jia-Xu Wang; Hao-Tai Cheng; Yecheng Shao; Wen Zhao; Gang Han; Yi-Jie Guo; Ren-Jing Xu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper investigates scaling behavior in offline RL, using task returns and model/data sweeps rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy and compute-matched fits.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling results for MambaDM. Baseline comparisons in Atari and D4RL, module ablations, initialization results, and return-to-go ablations are not rows because they do not test the claim versions. Figure 2's individual plotted values are not reliably attributable from the supplied text, so only the authors' stated aggregate findings are recorded for that figure.
record.test_reason: The paper runs a small 'scaling law' sweep of MambaDM in offline RL: layers 3–12, embedding 128–512, dataset 0.25M–1M. It reports only task returns, read from a figure. It gives no held-out loss, parameter counts, compute, or power-law fits, and every sweep spans less than one order of magnitude. Returns over this range cannot show whether a power-law form holds, so V5 is not tested. Downstream RL returns are not language-model downstream tasks (V6). The findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that increasing MambaDM's model size does not bring clear improvement in Atari/OpenAI Gym ('no definitive scaling law'), while larger datasets improve performance significantly. They recommend collecting larger and more diverse RL datasets, and caution that only two standard RL datasets were tested.
record.recipe_differences: This is an offline-RL task-performance sweep, not a held-out language-model cross-entropy scaling experiment; it does not fit power laws or compare compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance depends on the scale factor: model-size changes show fluctuations, while larger dataset amounts improve performance. Context length is also varied and described as yielding stable MambaDM performance.

fits_no_version.finding: In Atari and D4RL offline RL, MambaDM returns fluctuate without a clear upward trend as layers (3–12) or embedding dimension (128–512) increase. Returns improve as dataset size grows from 0.25M to 1M; the abstract says up to 33.7% for 2× data on Atari.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over small ranges in offline RL, task returns of a Mamba decision model do not rise reliably with model size but do rise with dataset size.

fits_no_version.finding: MambaDM Breakout scores across context lengths 10–60 (334.4, 365.4, 325.7, 313.2) are higher than DMamba's (231.6–295.9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MambaDM's Breakout score stays relatively stable across the tested context lengths.

record.problems: The scaling section reports task returns rather than held-out cross-entropy, gives no power-law fits or exponents, and does not test compute-optimal allocations. Figure 2's plotted values are not recoverable with reliable model/task attribution from the supplied text. Uncertainty for the scaling sweeps is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Individual task-by-factor values in Fig. 2 were not extracted because the supplied text does not allow reliable attribution of plotted values. Non-scaling benchmark comparisons and ablations are outside the claim versions.

untested.parts: Whether held-out loss follows a power law in parameters, data or compute in offline RL. No loss is reported, no fits are made, and ranges are under one order of magnitude.
Layers and width are varied, but not at fixed parameter count, and no loss is reported.

record.verdict_notes: Fig. 2 values cannot be read from the text, and no uncertainty is given for the sweeps. Table I lists context lengths 10, 30, 50, 80 and 100, but Table VI and Fig. 2 use 10–60, which is internally inconsistent. The '33.7%' in the abstract coincides with MambaDM's Frostbite score in Table II (33.7), so the figure is unverifiable. The reader's 'challenges' label on V5 is withdrawn, because the measure and range cannot bear on a power-law form of loss.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fits are extrapolated to larger runs.
No fixed-compute-budget comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is measured.
The paper does not compare architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
It studies offline RL task returns, not whether the same power-law form holds for held-out loss; it does not fit or report power-law exponents.
No downstream language-model task performance or relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss is measured.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits are compared across fitting choices or setups.

rows.subject: MambaDM
rows.operation_detail: Varied model-size-related settings and measured task performance.
rows.measure: RL task performance (returns/scores); the paper's qualitative summary of model-size scaling
rows.value: Performance fluctuates as model size increases; the authors report no clear upward trend or definitive scaling law.
rows.locator: Section V-A, Discussion; Fig. 2; Table I
rows.note: The paper gives this as an aggregate finding across the tested Atari and OpenAI Gym settings; individual plotted values are not recorded here.
rows.check: Measures RL returns, not loss, over 3–12 layers and 128–512 embedding (well under one order of magnitude), with no parameter counts. It cannot show or refute a power-law form. The 'absent' state overstates what the qualitative statement about Fig. 2 can show.

rows.subject: MambaDM
rows.operation_detail: Varied offline dataset amount and measured task performance.
rows.value: The authors report that increasing dataset size significantly improves performance; the abstract reports up to 33.7% score improvement on Atari when scaling dataset amount by 2×.
rows.locator: Abstract; Section V-A, Discussion; Fig. 2; Table I
rows.note: The reported improvement does not establish that the relationship follows a power law; the text does not specify which particular 2× comparison yields the maximum.
rows.check: Measures RL returns over only a 4× dataset range, with no fit. The abstract's 'up to 33.7%' is not traceable to any stated comparison.
